title: Air India 855
summary: Air India Flight 855 crashed into the Arabian Sea approximately one minute after takeoff from Mumbai on January 1, 1978, killing all 213 people aboard. The Boeing 747-237B, registered VT-EBD, experienced a loss of control during the right turn over the Arabian Sea. The captain's attitude direction indicator (ADI) had toppled but he misinterpreted the first officer's statement about his own toppled ADI, believing both indicated a right bank. Over the dark Arabian Sea with no external visual references, the captain made control inputs to increase the left bank, causing the aircraft to roll beyond recovery and crash into the sea.
probable_cause: Irrational control inputs by the captain following complete unawareness of the aircraft's attitude due to a malfunctioned ADI, with the crew failing to gain control using other flight instruments.

It was after sunset and the aircraft was flying over a dark Arabian Sea, leaving the aircrew unable to visually cross-check their ADI instrument readings with the actual horizon

title: Pacific Western Airlines 314
summary: Pacific Western Airlines Flight 314, a Boeing 737, crashed at Cranbrook Airport on February 11, 1978. The aircraft touched down about 800 feet from the runway threshold in snowing conditions with visibility of 3/4 mile. The pilots did not see a snowplow on the runway. To avoid collision, the captain immediately disengaged reverse thrust but one engine remained at idle reverse and the other at full forward thrust. The asymmetric thrust configuration rendered the aircraft uncontrollable. Calgary ATC had miscalculated the flight's arrival time. The aircraft crashed, killing 43 of 49 on board.
probable_cause: Asymmetric thrust reverser deployment after aborted landing to avoid snowplow, combined with ATC arrival time calculation error and crew failure to report beacon passage.

title: Continental Airlines 603
summary: Continental Airlines Flight 603 experienced cascading tire failures during takeoff roll from runway 6R when the recapped tread of the number-two tire on the left main landing gear separated, causing that tire to blow out. The overload caused the adjacent number-one tire to blow out immediately, and metal pieces from both rims damaged the number-five tire. Unable to stop on the wet runway, the aircraft overran the departure end and the left main gear collapsed, puncturing fuel tanks and causing a post-impact fire.
probable_cause: The aircraft could not stop within the runway confines due to cascading tire failures on the left main landing gear and partial loss of braking power. The number-two tire failed due to separation of its recapped tread. The tires may have been operated in an over-deflection condition due to suboptimal average inflation pressure for maximum gross weight.

title: Korean Air Lines 902
summary: A Korean Air Lines Boeing 707 en route from Paris to Seoul veered off course over the Arctic Ocean near the North Magnetic Pole causing large errors in the aircraft's magnetic compass-based navigation systems. The aircraft entered Soviet airspace near the Kola Peninsula at 21:19 UTC and was intercepted by a Soviet Su-15. After failing to follow the interceptor, a missile struck the left wing knocking off 4 metres and puncturing the fuselage. The crew successfully executed an emergency landing on the frozen Korpijärvi Lake with 107 survivors.

title: Pacific Southwest Airlines 182
summary: PSA Flight 182, a Boeing 727, collided mid-air with a Cessna 172 during approach to San Diego on a clear day with 10 miles visibility. The PSA crew lost visual contact with the Cessna despite ATC instructions to maintain visual separation and did not report the loss of sight. The NTSB determined the probable cause was the PSA flight crew's failure to follow proper air traffic control procedures.
probable_cause: The probable cause of the accident was the failure of the PSA flight crew to follow proper air traffic control procedures. Flight 182's crew lost sight of the Cessna in contravention of ATC instructions to keep visual separation from that traffic and did not alert ATC that they had lost sight of it. Errors on the part of ATC were also named as contributing factors, including the use of visual separation procedures when radar clearances were available.

title: Cessna 188 Pacific rescue
summary: A Cessna 188 delivering aircraft from the United States to Australia became lost over the Pacific Ocean when its automatic direction finder malfunctioned. The pilot, retired Navy pilot Jay Prochnow, declared an emergency after realizing he could not find Norfolk Island. Air New Zealand Flight 103, a McDonnell Douglas DC-10 with 88 passengers en route from Fiji to Auckland, was the only aircraft in the vicinity. The DC-10 captain, Gordon Vette, was a qualified navigator who calculated the Cessna's position using sunset geometry and heading differences. The DC-10 guided the Cessna to Norfolk Island, where it landed safely.

factors.evidence: The automatic direction finder had malfunctioned and the pilot realized he was now lost somewhere over the Pacific Ocean.
When Prochnow believed he was approaching Norfolk Island, he was unable to see the island and did not know his actual position over the Pacific.
Prochnow was a retired United States Navy pilot delivering a Cessna 188 from the United States to Australia.
The Cessna was guided to Norfolk Island by the DC-10 crew and landed safely with no fatalities.

events.text: On morning of December 20, pilot took off from Pago Pago en route to Norfolk Island.
Pilot believed approaching Norfolk Island but unable to see it; automatic direction finder had malfunctioned.
Pilot alerted ATC and declared emergency; only Air New Zealand DC-10 Flight 103 was in vicinity with 88 passengers.
DC-10 captain Gordon Vette, a qualified navigator, used sunset geometry and heading differences to calculate Cessna position and provide guidance.
Cessna successfully landed at Norfolk Island guided by DC-10 crew with no fatalities.

notes: No fatality accident; successful emergency rescue
Notable for creative navigation solution using sun position geometry
Outcome demonstrates crew coordination between civil and general aviation
Earlier Cessna on delivery flight crashed on takeoff at Pago Pago but pilot unharmed

title: United Airlines 173
summary: Flight 173 ran out of fuel during a prolonged hold caused by a landing gear problem. While the crew troubleshot the gear with the landing gear down and flaps extended, fuel consumption was greatly increased but not adequately monitored. Due to cockpit culture, the first officer and flight engineer failed to assertively communicate the critical fuel situation to the captain. All four engines flamed out due to fuel starvation, and the aircraft crashed in a suburban Portland area with 10 fatalities. This accident prompted the development of crew resource management training.
probable_cause: The flight crew became so absorbed with diagnosing the landing gear problem that they failed to monitor their fuel state and calculate a time when they needed to return to land or risk fuel exhaustion.

factors.evidence: The right main landing gear retract cylinder assembly had failed due to corrosion, allowing the right gear to free fall and damage a microswitch that prevented the green light from illuminating.
Due to cockpit culture at the time, the co-pilot and flight engineer failed to adequately convey the seriousness of the fuel situation to the captain.
The crew became so absorbed with diagnosing the landing gear problem that they failed to monitor their fuel state and calculate when they needed to land.
All four engines flamed out due to fuel starvation.
The aircraft crashed into a wooded section of northeast Portland about 6 nautical miles southeast of the airport.

events.text: Flight 173 departed Denver's Stapleton International Airport at 15:47 MST with 189 people on board and approximately 46,700 lb of fuel.
As the landing gear was being lowered on approach to Portland, the crew felt an abnormal vibration and yaw and the gear-down indicator light did not illuminate.
The crew requested a holding pattern to diagnose the landing gear problem with gear down and flaps at 15 degrees, greatly increasing fuel burn rate.
Engines 3 and 4 eventually flamed out due to fuel starvation.
Engines 1 and 2 quit due to fuel starvation flameouts; a mayday was declared.
The aircraft crashed into a wooded section about 6 nautical miles southeast of Portland airport.
